llmsa: Measurement System Analysis for Pipelines Built on Large Language Models

llmsa treats a pipeline built on a large language model (LLM) as what it is: a measurement procedure with unknown measurement uncertainty. It validates the pipeline with the methods that analytical and clinical laboratories have used for decades: a crossed precision study with variance components (gauge R&R), attribute agreement, bias against a reference, Plackett-Burman screening of robustness, simulation-based planning of the study size, Westgard-rule control charts for ongoing system suitability, and a validation report in the structure a reviewer or an auditor expects.

The object of the validation is always a concrete pipeline (model, prompt, settings) for a stated task and risk, never “the LLM” in general. Any pipeline qualifies whose output is a number, an ordered class or a yes/no answer; results produced outside R can be imported.

Why

Benchmarks report how often a model is right. A laboratory needs to know something else before it acts on a result: how much the result changes when the same question is asked again (repeatability), when it is asked in other words or of another model (reproducibility), whether it is systematically off (bias), whether a typo or a different number format changes it (robustness), and whether it still behaves the same way next month (system suitability). None of this is new. Measurement system analysis (AIAG MSA), CLSI EP05, ICH Q2(R2) and the Westgard rules answer exactly these questions for instruments. llmsa applies them to pipelines built on LLMs, whose answers vary even at temperature 0 and whose models can change without notice.

The validation report ties the evidence to a stated context of use, a model risk and acceptance criteria fixed in advance. This is the structure of the credibility assessment in the FDA’s 2025 draft guidance on AI in regulatory decision-making.

When to use it

  • Before deployment. A crossed study (items × prompt variants × models × replicates × blocks) shows where the variation comes from and whether the pipeline separates the items it has to separate.
  • After a change. A new model version, a reworded prompt, another provider or quantisation: repeat the study with the changed component and compare the result with the validated state.
  • In routine use. A small control set with known answers runs before each batch, and msa_control_chart() applies the Westgard rules to catch drift, for example after a silent model update.

What maps to what

Measurement system analysis LLM pipeline
Measurand What the pipeline reports: a number (IC50), an ordered class (ACMG/AMP tier), a yes/no finding
Part Item (variant, document, assay record)
Appraiser Prompt variant (semantically equivalent wording)
Instrument Model (provider, version, quantisation)
Trial / replicate Repeated call under identical conditions
Day / session Block (endpoints drift with load and time)
Repeatability Variance between replicate calls
Reproducibility Variance from prompt, model, block and their interactions
Part-to-part variation Variance between items, the signal to resolve
Reference standard Expert-curated answer
Robustness (ICH Q2) Plackett-Burman screening of formatting and context perturbations
Control sample Small set with known answers, run before each batch

How llmsa itself is validated

A statistics package for validation has to be validated itself. In llmsa, a passing test is not enough for a statistic to count as verified. Each one needs two independent pieces of evidence: a published value, a recalculation by a different route, or a live comparison with an established package. Where no closed-form answer exists, a simulation study decides; it is planned with the ADEMP scheme (Morris, White and Crowther, 2019) and reported with Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE). Reference values are stored in reference/anchors/ with source, page, value and tolerance and are never estimated. Edge cases and invariances are tested explicitly.

Component Status Evidence
Variance components, %GRR, % contribution, ndc and verdict (numeric) verified equal to the ANOVA estimators on balanced designs; AIAG worked example; published REML estimates for lme4’s Penicillin data; NIST StRD ANOVA datasets with certified values; live comparison with VCA, SixSigma and lme4
Ordinal and binary outcomes (latent scale) verified equal to direct fits with ordinal::clmm() and lme4::glmer(); latent ICC against rptR and performance; recovery of simulated components with MCSE
Bootstrap intervals (msa_boot()) verified quantiles equal to lme4::bootMer(); coverage measured in seven scenarios with MCSE
Robustness screening (Plackett-Burman, Lenth) implemented; validation in progress planned: generator rows of Plackett and Burman (1946), comparison with FrF2, the worked examples of Lenth (1989), false-alarm rate at the nominal level
Agreement (Cohen, Krippendorff), bias and linearity implemented; not yet validated planned: published values for every weighting and scale level, established packages, AIAG examples, simulated coverage
Westgard rules, simulator, study planning implemented; not yet validated planned: each rule exactly at its limit, false-alarm rates against Westgard et al. (1981), recovery of simulated components
Execution, parsers, backends, report implemented; not yet validated planned: an interrupted and resumed run gives the same store, parsers on random input, recorded real API responses, every number in the report equal to the object value

The test suite of the statistical core detects 92.8 % of 1,478 deliberately injected faults (mutation testing of R/fit.R and R/grr.R, threshold 80 %).

The article vignette("validation", package = "llmsa") reruns the reference comparisons when it is built and reads the simulation results from the stored runs. It needs no network, and no number in it is typed in by hand. The AIAG handbook data are protected and not distributed: the public build marks those rows as not rerun, and the complete comparison runs locally.

The simulation studies also produced findings that matter in practice. For ordinal and binary outcomes, the latent prompt and model components were underestimated in several scenarios. Percentile intervals for the integer-valued ndc cover more often than their nominal level. The validation article reports every scenario with its MCSE, and the help pages of msa_fit() and msa_boot() name the affected scenarios.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("DanielMoj/llmsa", dependencies = TRUE, build_vignettes = TRUE)

llmsa needs R 4.1 or later. The fitting engines are lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and ordinal (Christensen, 2026). Optional packages add features: httr2 (API backend), ellmer (chat objects), DBI and RSQLite (SQLite store), jsonlite (response metadata), rmarkdown with pandoc (report). The validation article uses VCA, SixSigma, rptR and performance as live comparisons, so building the vignettes needs dependencies = TRUE. Continuous integration runs R CMD check on Linux, macOS and Windows.

Quick start

Analyse a study

ic50_demo is a simulated numeric extraction with known variance components: 40 compounds, 3 prompt variants, 3 models, 3 replicates in each of 2 blocks.

library(llmsa)

fit <- msa_fit(ic50_demo, type = "numeric")
msa_grr(fit)
#> Gauge R&R of an LLM measurement system
#>   outcome: numeric; 40 items x 3 prompts x 3 models x 2 block(s), 2152 observations
#>  Source               Variance SD     % Contribution % Study Var
#>  Total gauge R&R      0.0425   0.2061 4.2 %          20.5 %
#>    Repeatability      0.0140   0.1184 1.4 %          11.8 %
#>    Reproducibility    0.0285   0.1687 2.8 %          16.8 %
#>      prompt           0.0049   0.0697 0.5 %          6.9 %
#>      model            0.0171   0.1309 1.7 %          13.0 %
#>      block (time)     0.0010   0.0319 0.1 %          3.2 %
#>      prompt:model     0.0000   0.0046 0.0 %          0.5 %
#>      item:prompt      0.0001   0.0092 0.0 %          0.9 %
#>      item:model       0.0053   0.0731 0.5 %          7.3 %
#>  Part-to-part (items) 0.9672   0.9835 95.8 %         97.9 %
#>  Total variation      1.0097   1.0048 100.0 %        100.0 %
#>
#>   total gauge R&R: 20.5 % of study variation (4.2 % contribution)
#>   number of distinct categories (ndc): 6
#>   ICC (items): 0.958
#>   verdict: MARGINAL  [basis: % study variation, thresholds 10 / 30]

The measurement system takes up 20.5 % of the study variation, between the AIAG thresholds of 10 % and 30 %, hence marginal. The model is the largest single source of reproducibility variance, and the pipeline still resolves six distinct categories of compounds.

Plan and run a study 

tiers <- c("Benign", "Likely benign", "VUS", "Likely pathogenic", "Pathogenic")

# items are the parts, prompt variants the appraisers, models the instruments
items <- data.frame(item_id = sprintf("v%02d", 1:30),
                    text    = sprintf("variant %02d", 1:30))
prompts <- c(concise = "Classify {text} into the five ACMG/AMP tiers. Answer with the tier only.",
             role    = "You are a clinical variant scientist. Give the ACMG/AMP tier of {text}.",
             terse   = "ACMG/AMP tier of {text}?")
design <- msa_design(items, prompts, models = c("model-a", "model-b", "model-c"),
                     reps = 3, blocks = 2, seed = 1)

# offline: a mock backend with known variance components
truth   <- setNames(seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = 30), items$item_id)
backend <- backend_mock(truth, levels = tiers, thresholds = c(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5), seed = 2)
runs <- msa_run(design, backend, parse = parse_choice(tiers, whole_word = TRUE),
                store = "runs.sqlite")

fit <- msa_fit(runs, type = "ordinal", levels = tiers)  # warns: two blocks, see Design notes
grr <- msa_grr(fit)
ag  <- msa_agreement(runs, levels = tiers, weights = "linear")
msa_report(grr, runs = runs, agreement = ag,
           cou = "Pre-classification of sequence variants for expert review",
           risk = "medium", acceptance = "%GRR < 30 %; Krippendorff's alpha >= 0.8",
           output_file = "validation_report.html")

parse_choice(whole_word = TRUE) matches whole phrases, prefers “Likely benign” over “Benign” and returns NA for an answer that names two classes. It does not read negations (“not pathogenic” parses as “Pathogenic”), so prompts should ask for the label alone. The store keeps every call as it arrives; resume = TRUE continues an interrupted study without repeating a call.

Run against real models

backend_openai_compatible() talks to any server with the OpenAI chat-completions API. Behind a router such as OpenRouter, the same model name can be served by different providers and quantisations, which would change the instrument between calls. Pin both and disallow fallbacks:

pinned <- function(endpoint, quantisation) {
  backend_openai_compatible("https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",
                            api_key = Sys.getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY"),
                            temperature = 0, seed = 20261024,
                            provider = list(order = list(endpoint),
                                            allow_fallbacks = FALSE,
                                            quantizations = list(quantisation)))
}
backends <- list(llama = pinned("coreweave/fp16", "fp16"),
                 qwen  = pinned("deepinfra/fp8", "fp8"),
                 sol   = backend_openai_compatible(temperature = NULL,  # model rejects temperature
                                                   reasoning_effort = "medium", seed = 20261024))
backend <- function(prompt, model, row) backends[[row$model_id]](prompt, model, row)

design <- msa_design(items, prompts,
                     models = c(llama = "meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct",
                                qwen  = "qwen/qwen3-32b", sol = "gpt-6.1-sol"),
                     reps = 3, blocks = 2, seed = 1)
msa_run(design, backend, parse = parse_choice(tiers, whole_word = TRUE),
        block = 1, store = "study.sqlite")                     # day 1
runs <- msa_run(design, backend, parse = parse_choice(tiers, whole_word = TRUE),
                store = "study.sqlite", resume = TRUE)         # day 2: runs block 2, returns all

Each call is stored with its timestamp, block and run position, the model identifier, a hash of the rendered prompt, the raw response, the parsed value, latency and any error. From the API response the store keeps the response ID, the reported model snapshot, token usage, the system fingerprint, the finish reason and, where the endpoint returns them, the serving provider and the reasoning text; from the request, the provider order, quantisations, the fallback setting, seed, temperature, reasoning effort and timeout. Credentials and headers are never stored. msa_run(parse_by_prompt = ...) sets a parser per prompt variant, for example parse_json_field() for a prompt that asks for JSON.

Results from another pipeline

Results from Python, a workflow engine or a spreadsheet are analysed the same way once they have one row per call:

runs <- as_msa_runs(results, item = "doc_id", prompt = "prompt", model = "model",
                    rep = "replicate", value = "answer")

The ClinVar article takes this route, with ClinVar submitters as appraisers.

Step Functions
Plan a crossed study msa_design()
Plan the study size by simulation msa_simulate(), msa_plan()
Run it with an audit trail, resume after interruption msa_run()
Backends backend_openai_compatible(), backend_ellmer(), backend_mock()
Parsers parse_choice(), parse_number(), parse_json_field(), parse_identity()
Import results from elsewhere as_msa_runs()
Realised cell counts of a study msa_counts()
Variance components, numeric / ordinal / binary msa_fit()
Gauge R&R statistics, verdict, bootstrap intervals msa_grr(), msa_boot()
Attribute agreement and accuracy (Krippendorff, 2011; Cohen, 1960, 1968) msa_agreement()
Bias and linearity msa_bias()
Robustness screening (Lenth’s method) pb_design(), msa_robustness()
Ongoing system suitability (Westgard rules) msa_control_chart()
Validation report msa_report()

Articles

  • vignette("llmsa"), Validating an LLM pipeline as a measurement system: a complete validation, offline with the mock backend.
  • vignette("validation"), Statistical validation of llmsa: every comparison with published values, NIST certified values, package oracles and the simulation studies.
  • vignette("llm-stability"), Answer stability at temperature zero: 82,850 recorded calls of five models on eight tasks in ten runs, from the public llm-stability data of Atıl et al. (2025, Apache-2.0); attribute repeatability, hit rate and the share of missing answers per task and model.
  • vignette("clinvar-raters"), ClinVar submitters as a rater study: submitters as appraisers, with Krippendorff’s alpha and ordinal variance components for 1,383 variants in four genes of hereditary recurrent fevers (MEFV, MVK, NLRP3, TNFRSF1A) and a genome-wide sample of 1,000 variants, from public-domain ClinVar data (Landrum et al., 2025).

None of the articles calls a model. The real-data subsets they read are frozen under inst/extdata/ with SHA-256 checksums and their provenance; the scripts in data-raw/ rebuild them from the original sources. The simulated datasets ic50_demo and acmg_demo carry their true variance components as an attribute.

Design notes

  • Replicates must be spread in time. Identical requests at temperature 0 can return different completions because the load on the server, and with it the batch size, changes the order of floating-point operations (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Five calls within one second underestimate repeatability; use blocks and run them on different days.
  • Pin the instrument. Fix provider, quantisation and model snapshot, and record what the endpoint reports. A model name alone does not identify an instrument.
  • Few levels, wide intervals. Three models and four prompt variants are three and four levels of a random effect. Their variance components are estimated with large uncertainty, fits are often singular, and for ordinal and binary outcomes the simulation studies found these components underestimated in several scenarios. Report bootstrap intervals (msa_boot()) and plan the study (msa_plan()); the number of prompt variants, not the number of items, drives the precision of the reproducibility estimate.
  • Two levels are not enough for a variance. In an ordinal fit, a prompt, model or block factor with exactly two levels enters as a fixed effect, and its component is estimated by the range method beta-hat^2 / 2, which is biased upwards. msa_fit() warns and marks the component.
  • On the latent scale, repeatability is fixed, not measured. For ordinal and binary outcomes the residual variance is set by the link (1 for probit, pi^2/3 for logit; Nakagawa, Johnson and Schielzeth, 2017). The observed agreement between replicates comes from msa_agreement().
  • Memorisation confounds accuracy, not precision. Reference answers that are public (ClinVar, textbooks) may be in the training data. Use items added after the model’s knowledge cut-off for the accuracy question; the precision statistics are unaffected.
  • Acceptance criteria follow model risk. The AIAG thresholds (10 % and 30 % of study variation) are defaults, not laws. Set them from the consequence of a wrong decision in the stated context of use.
  • Free-text outcomes judged by a second model are a second measurement system that needs its own validation (a nested MSA). This release covers numeric, ordinal and binary outcomes.

Application study

The first application under way is the five-tier ACMG/AMP classification of sequence variants (Richards et al., 2015) against expert classifications: 100 variants, 3 prompt variants, 3 models via APIs (one proprietary, two open-weight with pinned provider and quantisation), 3 replicates in each of 2 blocks, 5,400 calls in the main study, plus a pilot and a robustness screen. The plan, the frozen item set and the runner are in inst/validation/ap1/. The plan was approved before the first call, and every later change is documented in a decision record. Results will be reported when the analysis is complete.

How llmsa is developed

Changes are built in milestones from written specifications. One model implements, a second reviews and owns the acceptance tests and reference values, a third writes adversarial end-to-end and fuzz tests, and only deterministic gates (R CMD check, the test suites, mutation testing) decide whether a milestone passes. The maintainer approves the specifications and every decision record. Specifications and decision records are in docs/ (in German); AGENTS.md, BACKLOG.md, PROGRESS.md, orchestrator/ and the other process files are excluded from the package build. The 22 exported functions of version 0.1.0 keep their interfaces; a change requires a decision record and a deprecation period.

Roadmap

  • Validation of the remaining components (agreement, bias and linearity, robustness, control charts, planning, execution and report) to the standard above.
  • Comparison of model versions as fixed levels, for revalidation after a change.
  • Sensitivity per class with a lower confidence bound, for decisions where one error direction matters more.
  • Bootstrap intervals for ordinal fits; modified-large-sample intervals for variance components (Burdick, Borror and Montgomery, 2003).
  • Batched multi-item prompts: position and carry-over effects analysed as in a crossover study (Williams designs).
  • Nested validation of LLM-as-judge scoring for free-text outcomes.
  • Detection-limit style experiments: how much evidence a document must contain before a finding is extracted reliably.
  • First release with a Zenodo DOI, then CRAN.
